doc.title: Sonny Rollins — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Why the 'Body and Soul' solo was so hard and why it broke through
summary: He explains the technical and harmonic difficulty of Hawkins's solo and wonders why it became the hit.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Coleman Hawkins and the great saxophonists

blocks.x: Well, that was a hard solo. It was, um...they had transcriptions of it. They had everything of it. People we’re trying to play that, you know. I played some of it, but it was a difficult solo to really get. I don’t think I ever played the whole solo, you know.
What do you think it difficult about it?

Well, just technically it’s difficult. There’s technically a lot of uh um, things that–you know, this is many years later, but at that time when that was made–1939, I believe–there were a lot of uh uh, ways that the saxophone was played, which were revolutionary at that time, and he was doing them. So, uh there were a lot of technical feats which he accomplished with that solo.
Are you talking about intervals, or are you talking about harmonically, or...?

Well, I’m talking about, um, technically: just playing the instrument itself. Now, as far as what he played, yes, what he played was also highly advanced. He was playing a lot of uh very advanced stuff, you know. And uh, but beyond that it was just so technical to play some of the runs and things that he made on the horn was, it was quite formidable.
Hm. He made lots of great recordings...
Why do you think Body and Soul is the one that broke through?

I don’t know. Well, I’m like Monk, I don’t why that one made it. How did you make a solo that got everyone’s attention, and you were playing all this advanced music? [laughing] All this stuff, and there was no melody. There was no words. Just this really saxophone virtuoso, you know, playing. You know, I mean, how did it, how did it work, but it worked.
